Aerial Wildlife Survey Report  
Wildlife Management Unit 320 Aerial Ungulate Survey for Moose 
(2018) 
 
Background 
An aerial ungulate survey for moose was conducted in December 2018 in Wildlife Management Unit (WMU) 320 
using transect survey methodology. This WMU is located in the Lower Foothills Natural Region of west central 
Alberta and is 878 km2. Prior to 2018, WMU 320 was surveyed in 1999, 2002 and 2012 using a random stratified 
block methodology. The population and density estimates were determined as a proportion of the total survey 
based on WMU area.  
 
During the 2018 aerial survey, sightings of white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were recorded and population 
estimates were completed for these three species as well using transect survey methodology. Population 
estimates for white-tailed deer and mule deer were calculated previously for WMU 320 during the 1999, 2002 and 
2012 aerial surveys, however no previous population estimates for elk were completed. Previous year’s population 
and density estimates for white-tailed deer are provided in Table 2 and population and density estimates for mule 
deer are provided in Table 3. All of these above observations were recorded and entered into the Fisheries and 
Wildlife Management Information System (FWMIS) at the completion of the survey.  
 
In WMU 320, the antlered and antlerless moose archery only season runs from September 1 to  October 31 and the 
general (rifle) season runs from November 1 to 30. Both the archery only and the general (rifle) require Special 
Licences obtained through the Special Licence application process.   
 
Hunter harvest data in WMU 320 for moose Special Licences indicate five-year (2014 to 2018) average success as 
follows: antlered moose 71% and antlerless moose 50%.  Over the past five-years on average; 13 Antlered Moose 
Special Licences were issued annually and 7 Special Licences annually were issued for ant lerless moose.  
 
The primary objectives of this survey were to assess the status of moose populations in WMU 320 by determining 
a population estimate based on density estimates, and a population demographic split for sex and age classes.  
The secondary objectives of this survey were to assess the status of white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk 
populations in WMU 320 by determining a population estimate based on density estimates, and a population 
demographic split for sex and age classes. 
 
Survey Method 
 
The transect survey was conducted flying east-west lines at 1.6 km (1 mile) intervals, with 25% coverage (400 
metre wide survey strip) on December 8, 2018 and was completed with 7.0 hours of flight time. At each 
observation point, we counted moose and we determined sex and age and verified that each observation was 
within the transect width. For white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk we classified each observation for sex and age 
class, but did not record antler size. 
   
Because transects varied in length (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969), we calculated the average density (R; #/km 2) of 
moose by summing the total animals counted per transect (∑x) by total area searched (length of transects 
multiplied by 400 metre survey strip [∑z]). For a population estimate (unequal sized units, sampling without 
replacement), we multiplied the average density (R) by the overall area of the WMU (Z). No correction factor was 
applied for moose population estimates. We calculated the width of the 90% c onfidence interval by multiplying the t 
statistic for the left-tailed inverse of the Student’s t-distribution, (t0.05,df=n-1) by standard error (SE; without 
replacement) of the abundance estimate where SE=sq root variance, and variance=N*(N -n)/(n*(n-1))*(∑x2+R2*∑z2-
2*R*∑xz) with N as the total number of possible transects given 100% coverage, and n as the number of transects 
sampled.

Results 
 
For WMU 320, we surveyed 23 transects out of a possible 92 on December 8, 2018 for a total survey effort of 545 
km of transects and a survey area of 218 km2 (24.83% of WMU). In total, we counted 117 moose from 52 groups.  
 
Of the 117 moose that were classified:  
 
 29 (25%) were bulls 
 56 (48%) were cows 
 32 (27%) were calves 
 
The bull:cow and calf:cow ratios were 0.52 and 0.57, respectively. The final density estimate was 0.54/km 2 with a 
90% confidence interval of 0.35/km2 to 0.72 km2. This corresponds to a 90% confidence interval that is +/- 35% of 
the density estimate. The estimated moose abundance is 471 (306, 636). We estima ted the 2018 post-hunting 
season winter moose population split to be 117 bulls, 226 cows, and 127 calves. The 2018 moose survey results 
and previous survey population and density estimates for moose are provided in Table 1.   
 
Table 1. Previous density, and age/sex composition ratios for moose in WMU 320. Survey types have 
included random stratified block (RSB), and transect sampling methods.  
Year Survey Type Population Estimate Moose/km2 +/-% Bull:cow:calf 
1999 RSB 293 0.33 21.8 26:100:53 
2002 RSB 395 0.44 22.5 75:100:68 
2012 RSB 271 0.31 16.2 69:100:64 
2018 Transect  471 0.54 33.5 52:100:57 
 
Survey effort parameters for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk were identical to what was surveyed for moose 
and outlined above. Population estimates were calculated for white-tailed deer, mule deer and elk using the same 
methodology as outlined for moose (see Krebs 2014, Jolly 1969) for transects of varying lengths.  
  
A total of 168 white-tailed deer were observed in 52 groups. Of the white-tailed deer classified observed there 
were: 
 
 15(9%) bucks 
 98 (58%) does 
 55 (33%) fawns 
 
The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were .15 and .56 respectively. The final density estimate for white-tailed deer 
was 0.54 /km2 for a final post-hunting season winter estimate of 677 white-tailed deer.  
 
We estimated the post-hunting season winter population split to be 61 bucks, 393 does and 223 fawns.

Table 2. Previous density, and age/sex composition ratios for white-tailed deer in WMU 320. Survey types 
have included random stratified block (RSB), and transect sampling methods. 
Year Survey Type Population Estimate WTDE/km2 buck:doe:fawn 
1999 RSB 510 0.57 NA 
2002 RSB 1,293 1.44 NA 
2018 Transect  677 0.77 15:100:56 
 
A total of 30 mule deer were observed in six groups. Of the mule deer classified observed there were:  
 
 8 (27%) bucks 
 15 (50%) does 
 7 (23%) fawns 
 
The buck:doe and fawn:doe ratios were .53 and .47 respectively. The final density estimate for mule deer was 0.14 
/km2 for a final post-hunting season winter estimate of 121 mule deer.  
 
We estimated the post-hunting season winter population split to be 33 bucks, 60 does and 28 fawns. The 
population estimate should be used cautiously due to the low number and groups of mule deer observed during 
the survey.   
 
Table 3. Previous density, and age/sex composition ratios for mule deer in WMU 320. Survey types have 
included random stratified block (RSB), and transect sampling methods. 
Year Survey Type Population Estimate MUDE/km2 buck:doe:fawn 
1999 RSB 414 0.46 NA 
2002 RSB 436 0.49 NA 
2018 Transect  121 0.14 53:100:47 
 
A total of 167 elk were observed in three groups, which included a group of 125 elk. Due to the low number of 
groups (3) of elk which were observed it is problematic to provide a statistically reliable population estimate for elk.   
 
Based on surveying 25% of the WMU, and observing 167 elk, a simplistic density estimate 0.77 elk/km2 which 
equates to a population estimate of 673 elk. Of the 167 elk observed there were 1 bull, 9 cows and 4 calves 
classified in one group. 
 
The remaining elk were not classified due to the location and size of the observed groups.  There has been no 
previous population estimate for elk in WMU 320 during any of the previous aerial surveys.
